haiku-low.q1: They do not differ. Unknown email and wrong password follow one path, use a dummy bcrypt hash, and return an identical 401 body and headers.
haiku-low.q2: It gets a 429 'Too many failed attempts' response with Retry-After 900, and no password check runs. The lock lasts 15 minutes.
haiku-low.q3: On successful login the old session is destroyed and a new one is created under a fresh ID. On failed login the old session stays live.
haiku-low.q4: Only a random session ID, in the __Host-sid cookie. It is HttpOnly, so page scripts cannot read it.
haiku-low.q5: The session stops at 12 hours after creation, even with constant activity. The 30-minute idle timeout restarts on each request.
haiku-low.q6: It deletes the key, returns nil, redirects 302 to /login, and clears the cookie. Missing, unknown, expired and malformed sessions get the same response.
haiku-low.q7: The server deletes the session key before responding, then sends 303 to /login with the cookie cleared. If the key is already gone, the response is the same.
haiku-low.q8: Sessions live in shared Redis. Any instance looks up sess:sha256(id) there, so both instances see the same state.
haiku-low.q9: In Redis, in a sorted set fails:sha256(email) of timestamps from Redis TIME. Each FAIL trims entries older than 10 minutes, so only recent ones count.
haiku-low.q10: It compares Redis TIME with created_at against the 12-hour limit. When valid, it sets the key TTL to min(30 min, time left to 12 hours).
haiku-low.q11: A 503 login page with no cookie change. The old session is either intact or already destroyed, and the user must retry.
haiku-low.q12: Redis key TTLs remove them: idle sessions expire after 30 minutes, and every session expires by 12 hours. No sweeper or cron job is used.

sonnet.q1: They do not differ. Both follow one code path (unknown email is compared against a dummy bcrypt hash of the same cost) and get an identical 401 body and headers ("Invalid email or password").
sonnet.q2: The failures are counted in a sliding window, so the fifth failure sets a 15-minute lock. That fifth failure itself returns 401. Later attempts get 429 ("Too many failed attempts. Try again in 15 minutes.", Retry-After 900), with no password check and no bcrypt. Attempts during the lock are not counted and do not extend it. Caveat: attempts already past the lock check when the fifth failure lands are still verified, up to 13 verifications per cycle.
sonnet.q3: On success, LOGIN_OK deletes the old session the cookie pointed to (even if the new login is for a different user) and creates a new session under a fresh ID. The incoming ID is never reused. The browser gets Set-Cookie with the new ID. On a failed login (401, 429 or 503), the old session stays live.
sonnet.q4: The cookie `__Host-sid` holds only a random session ID (32 bytes from a CSPRNG, base64url). It is HttpOnly, so page scripts cannot read it. It is also Secure, SameSite=Lax, Path=/, with no Domain.
sonnet.q5: At the 12-hour absolute limit, measured from created_at. The idle timeout is 30 minutes and is restarted on each request, so it does not trigger. The next request after 12 hours finds the session deleted, gets a 302 to /login, and has the cookie cleared. Redis may also drop the key at the 12-hour mark because the TTL is min(30 min, time left).
sonnet.q6: The TOUCH script returns nil, and the app sends a 302 redirect to /login and clears the cookie. The client cannot tell missing, unknown, expired and malformed apart. The Redis key is deleted if it exists and is expired or malformed.
sonnet.q7: If a cookie is present, the app runs DEL on sess:sha256(sid) in Redis before responding. If there is no cookie, it just sends a 303 to /login. If the key is already gone (including already expired), that counts as success: 303 to /login with the cookie cleared. If the delete errors, it returns 503 with the cookie kept.
sonnet.q8: In Redis (7.x, one primary plus one async replica, not Cluster), shared by both app instances. The key is sess:<sha256(session ID)> and the value is a hash {user_id, created_at}. Whichever instance gets the request hashes the cookie's session ID and looks up that key in the shared Redis (via the TOUCH script).
sonnet.q9: In Redis, in a sorted set `fails:<h>`, where h = sha256 of the trimmed, lowercased email. Each entry is a failure timestamp from Redis TIME plus a unique nonce. The set has a 10-minute TTL. On each FAIL, the script adds the entry, trims entries older than 10 minutes, and counts what remains. That makes a true sliding window.
sonnet.q10: It compares the session hash's created_at against Redis TIME "now": valid only if user_id is non-empty, created_at is an integer and created_at <= now, and 12h - (now - created_at) is greater than 0. When valid, it writes back a PEXPIRE on the key of min(30 min, remaining absolute time) and returns user_id. There is no last-seen field.
sonnet.q11: A Redis error on LOGIN_OK gives a 503 login page with no cookie change. The outcome is unknown: either the old session is intact, or it was already destroyed and the new one was never delivered. The user retries.
sonnet.q12: The Redis key TTL alone. Abandoned sessions expire (idle 30 min, or at the 12-hour mark through the min() TTL). There is no sweeper, no cron job, and nothing in Postgres to clean.
